title: Prajna Paramita 2 Vedana
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes that our habitual tendency to label experiences as good or bad can be a powerful tool for self-awareness and liberation. By recognizing this pattern, we can begin to see reality in a more nuanced way, beyond our usual notions of right and wrong. This understanding is rooted in the concept of Prajnaparamita, which suggests that there may be more to existence than our ordinary perceptions, and invites us to explore this idea further.

Instantly I had a negative feeling.
The feeling seemed to first be noticed by me as a thought.
It seemed like, "Oh no, I'm woke up in the middle of the night.

Maybe there's a little feeling of fear.
I wouldn't get back to sleep.
Maybe some projection into the future: it's going to mess up my whole day tomorrow or something like that.
Do you know this?
Although fortunately I'm actually a pretty steady sleeper these days.
I just breathe a little bit and settle back down.
I went back to sleep.
I survived my own mind.
Then later I woke up again.
Again that "oh no" feeling arose.
Then I looked at the clock and I saw it was 5:40 a.m., just a few minutes before the alarm was set to go off.
My mind quickly reorganized itself and I had the thought, "Oh, it's good I'm awake right now.
Perfect."
So we have good and bad, fortunate and unfortunate.
We can really see the power of the mind to so quickly ascribe negative reactions to things.
Once in a while, in a lucky moment, positive reactions are instantly popped into the mind.
There's always some connection, it seems, to some experience, but the connection is often tenuous at best.
This rapid pulling away from our actual experience in that moment into some complex of emotion, thought, worry, memory, planning, judgment, and how quickly that happens.

So I've always really appreciated the early Buddhist teachings that put a lot of weight and importance in the study of this aspect of mind, which doesn't get as much airplay in Western psychology, I don't think, at least my understanding of Western psychology.
It's a great contribution of Buddhist psychology, I think, to the discourse about how to work with the mind.
They have this whole aspect of mind that they called Vedana, a Pali word; the Sanskrit word is almost identical.
This quality of mind, this ability of the mind is so quickly, even before thought is the idea.
The idea is that this Vedana feeling, this negative feeling when I woke up, first happens before thoughts accumulate to try to explain it and make sense of it and justify it.
Vedana is usually translated as feelings or, slightly better, feeling tone, but there's not really a good word in English for this tendency of mind to rapidly sort things into positive and negative.
I'm always talking about Vedana, so you've probably heard this part before, but it's important to study it, it's liberating.

And then we can study the power of that initial leaning in or away, of that judgment, how quickly it cascades down through our thought process and into our story, and into our story, and how caught we can get in that story.
